title: Let them be new (7:8)
hookLine: it's forbidden to remind someone who has returned of their past
tomorrow: if there's a world to come, do we bring our bodies?

cards: There's a story that comes out at every holiday dinner. The time your cousin set the kitchen on fire. The time someone got lost at the zoo.
Everyone laughs. Usually. But once someone has truly changed, can you still tell the story of what they did?
Maimonides answers, and his rule is stricter than a family dinner might guess.

teach.h: IF FOOLS TAUNT, LET IT GO.
teach.b: People who return, he writes, are humble. If fools taunt them, yesterday you did this and that, they should let it go. Then he turns to everyone else, and the tone sharpens.
It is utterly forbidden to say to someone who has returned: remember what you used to do. Forbidden to bring it up in front of them to shame them.
Even forbidden to mention things connected to it, hints that steer them back to the memory.
He files all of this under a Torah law, ona'at devarim, wronging someone with words; Leviticus says not to wrong one another. The Mishnah gives this exact example.
Here's the surprise to pass on: in this law, a joke can be the violation. Not a lie, not a curse. Just a reminder.
The old story may be true. It just isn't who they are now. Take smell.
After a burnt dinner, a kitchen holds the smoke for days.
Open the windows, cook something new, and slowly the room changes. Someone who has turned is doing that work. Every time the old story comes out, the windows close again.

how: Jewish law counts hurtful words as ona'at devarim, a real wrong; Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10 names reminding a returner of their past as an example, and it's taught in study of the laws of speech.

games.q: what does “let them be new” mean?
o: give a fresh start only after it's been proven
don't remind someone who changed of their past
forget a person's wrongs once they apologize

p: forbidden to bring up the past

s: it's fine to joke about someone's past if the story is true
true or not, reminding someone who returned of their past is wronging with words.
even hints that steer back to the old deed are forbidden
Maimonides includes mentioning things connected to it.
the rule mostly protects returners from lies about them
the old story isn't false. the rule protects them from the truth used against them.

games.q: your friend used to copy homework; she stopped a year ago. in a study group someone says, 'just copy off her, she's a pro.' what's the 7:8 move?
o: laugh it off; it's only a joke, and it's true.
move the talk along, and later tell the joker that line stings.
remind everyone she's changed, so they know her whole story.
games.why: a joke can be ona'at devarim. even 'she's changed' retells the old story; the cleaner move is not to bring it up at all.

practice: If there's water nearby, pour a little and take one slow sip, tasting it as if it were the first water you'd ever had.
Then breathe in through your nose and notice what the room smells like right now, not this morning, not last week. Let the present be the only thing in your mouth and your lungs.

wordCard.voice: Let them be new: Maimonides' rule. You may not remind someone who has returned of who they used to be.

orig.note: Hebrew: wronging with words, the law Maimonides files this under.

carryVoice: Something to keep: let them be new; the old story may be true, but it isn't theirs anymore. Twenty-one down, nine to go.

sources.ref: Mishneh Torah, Laws of Return (Hilkhot Teshuvah) 7:8 (returners are humble and let taunts go; forbidden to say 'remember your former deeds', to shame them, or to hint at it; ona'at devarim)
Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10 (one may not say to a returner, remember your former deeds)
